items.title: Writing in plain English
items.source: GOV.UK Style Guide; Content design guidance
items.body: Government writing should be clear to anyone who reads it. Use short sentences and common words. Say 'send' not 'forward', 'help' not 'facilitate', 'before' not 'prior to'. Use the active voice: 'The team sent the letter' is clearer than 'The letter was sent by the team'. Put the main point first, say what you need the reader to do and by when. Avoid jargon and abbreviations or explain them the first time. Check names, dates and figures. Read your writing aloud and cut every word that does not earn its place. Clear writing is a core skill in almost every Civil Service role because the people you write to are often anxious, busy or not familiar with the system.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is written in the plainest English?

options.text: Kindly ensure the aforementioned documentation is submitted forthwith.
It is requested that the form be tendered prior to the stipulated date.
Documentation should be facilitated by the end of the working week.
Please send us your form by Friday.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is in the active voice?

options.text: The letter was sent by the team.
Sending of the letter was done.

questions.prompt: Which is the best email subject line to ask a customer for proof of address by 5 November?

options.text: Action needed by 5 November: send proof of address
Important, please read as soon as it is convenient

questions.prompt: Rewrite in plain English: 'Pursuant to the aforementioned provisions, claimants are required to furnish documentary evidence of their residential address at the earliest opportunity.'
questions.answer: For example: 'You need to send us proof of your address as soon as you can.' It uses short, common words, talks directly to the reader, and says what to do. A fuller version could add what counts as proof and how to send it.
questions.rubric: Should be shorter, use everyday words, address the reader as you, and state the action clearly.

items.title: Emails and letters to the public
items.source: GOV.UK Style Guide; Civil Service Code
items.body: When you write to a customer or colleague, think about who they are and what they need. Open with the main point. If someone is upset, acknowledge it first and say what you will do next, for example 'I am sorry you have had this problem. I am looking into it now and will update you by Thursday.' Do not be defensive and do not promise what you cannot deliver. Before you send, check the recipient, the attachments and any personal information. 'Reply all' should be used only when everyone needs the answer. Keep a record of what you sent. Use a tone that is polite, direct and kind.

questions.prompt: When should you use 'Reply all' on an email?

options.text: Only when everyone on the email needs to see your reply

questions.prompt: A customer writes to you upset about a delay. Which opening is best?

options.text: You should have contacted us sooner.
I am sorry for the delay. I am checking your case now and will update you by Thursday.

questions.prompt: What should you check before sending a letter that contains personal data?

options.text: That the address and the attachments are correct and for the right person
That the font matches the template

questions.prompt: Write a short, polite reply to a customer who has asked for something your department cannot do.
questions.answer: For example: 'Dear Ms Khan, thank you for your letter of 3 November. I am sorry that I cannot arrange this, because the rules do not allow it for your type of claim. You can ask for a review by writing to us within one month, or call the number on this letter and we will explain how. I hope this helps. Yours sincerely, [your name].' It thanks, explains in plain words, says what the customer can do next and gives a contact.
questions.rubric: Should be polite, clear, explain the reason briefly, give next steps and a contact, and avoid blame or jargon.

items.title: Spreadsheet basics
items.source: Microsoft Excel basics; common office practice
items.body: Many entry roles use spreadsheets such as Excel to list cases, track work and check figures. A spreadsheet is a grid of cells. Columns have letters and rows have numbers, so B3 is column B, row 3. Formulas start with an equals sign. =SUM(B2:B6) adds the cells from B2 to B6. =AVERAGE(C2:C9) gives the mean of those cells. You can sort a list, filter it to show only some rows and freeze the top row so headings stay in view. Check formulas by working a few figures by hand and keep a copy before making big changes. Keep personal data in a spreadsheet secure, store it only where it is allowed and share it only with people who need it.

questions.prompt: In a spreadsheet, what does the cell reference B3 mean?

options.text: The third cell of the first row

questions.prompt: Which formula adds the cells from B2 to B6?
Which formula gives the average of the cells C2 to C9?
Cell B2 contains 200 and cell B3 contains 50. What does =B3/B2*100 give?

items.title: Handling information safely
items.source: Government Security Classifications; UK GDPR and Data Protection Act 2018
items.body: Civil servants handle information that matters to people and to the country. Government information is marked with a security classification: OFFICIAL, SECRET or TOP SECRET. Most work is OFFICIAL, and it is still not for sharing outside the job. Data protection law says personal information must be used lawfully, fairly and only for the reason it was collected, kept accurate and kept secure. You must not look at records without a work reason, even for friends or family. Misusing personal data can be a criminal offence and a disciplinary matter. If you lose something, find a mistake or see information left unprotected, report it straight away through your department's security process. Reporting quickly is always better than hoping nobody notices.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a UK government security classification?
What does data protection law require of personal data?

options.text: It can be shared with anyone
It may be kept forever for any purpose
It must be used lawfully and fairly, only as needed, and kept secure
It only applies to paper records

questions.prompt: You find a printout with customers' details in the staff kitchen. What is the best action?

options.text: Put it in a normal bin
Take it home to deal with it later
Secure it and report it through the department's security process

questions.prompt: A neighbour asks you to look up the status of their benefit claim on the department's system. What do you do?
questions.answer: Refuse. Looking up a record without a work reason is unauthorised access: it breaches data protection law and the Civil Service Code, can be a criminal offence and is likely to lead to disciplinary action. Explain kindly that you cannot do it and suggest they contact the department or use their own account. If you are put under pressure, tell your line manager.
questions.rubric: Should refuse, explain it is unauthorised access (law, Code, discipline), stay kind, point to proper routes and mention telling a manager if pressured.
